title: Asma Khan Challenges Fine Dining's Double Standard on Indian Cuisine
excerpt: The Darjeeling Express chef and Netflix star pushes back against the persistent perception that Indian food doesn't deserve a place at the fine-dining table.
body:
• Asma Khan, chef-owner of London's Darjeeling Express, has spent nearly a decade challenging the entrenched view that Indian food is inherently "cheap and cheerful"
  • Her restaurant, staffed entirely by women home cooks, holds a Michelin Guide listing and was recently named an OpenTable Icon
  • Khan's upcoming SOAS lecture on food politics will address the power dynamics and exploitation behind Western culinary trends
  • As Darjeeling Express prepares to move to a larger Rupert Street location, Khan continues advocating for immigrant women in hospitality

The Price of Respect

Asma Khan has spent nearly a decade asking a question the London restaurant industry would rather avoid: why are diners happy to pay £95 for a French or Japanese tasting menu but balk at the same price for Indian food?

The chef and owner of Darjeeling Express — the first British chef to feature on Netflix's Chef's Table — has made that question the foundation of her culinary career. When she introduced one of London's most expensive Indian tasting menus, the reaction proved her point.

"People are happy to pay £95 for a French, Italian or Spanish tasting menu, maybe Japanese, but would ask 'why is an Indian tasting menu at that price?' It's at that price because it deserves to be."

— Asma Khan, Chef and Owner, Darjeeling Express

"It's a very ancient cuisine. There are a lot of layers and heritage and techniques in the way we cook but somehow this has not been explained properly," Khan told Restaurant Online. The prejudice, she argues, runs deeper than pricing — it reflects how British society views the immigrants who brought the food.

From Supper Club to Michelin Guide

Khan's trajectory is itself a rebuke to the establishment. Born in India and trained as a constitutional lawyer with a PhD in British Constitutional Law, she arrived in Britain in 1991 to a hostile reception — she has described having to cycle fast to dodge bottles thrown at her on the street. She couldn't cook when she first moved to London and returned to India to learn family recipes before launching supper clubs in her home.

By 2017, she had opened Darjeeling Express in Soho with an all-female kitchen staffed not by culinary school graduates but by former nannies and cleaners she had befriended. Industry professionals told her she would fail. Instead, the restaurant earned a Michelin Guide listing, and Khan landed on Time magazine's 100 most influential people list. In 2024, she won the Johannes van Dam Prize, a lifetime-achievement award for contributions to gastronomy. She has served as a UN World Food Programme chef advocate since 2022.

Her third cookbook, Monsoon, focuses on seasonal cooking — another deliberate challenge to industry norms. "I don't want a jet-lagged okra on my menu. I don't want the air miles and the carbon footprint," she told Reuters earlier this year. "So I gracefully say no, we go by the seasons in Britain."

Structural Barriers Beyond the Menu

Khan's critique extends beyond pricing to the structural racism that keeps immigrant and female chefs on the margins. She has spoken repeatedly about how landlords refused to lease premium sites to her despite a proven track record — a prejudice she compares to arranged-marriage dynamics.

"Someone who looks like me, talks like me, has an all-female kitchen, our shadows would not have crossed," she told Restaurant Online about eventually securing the former Carluccio's flagship in Covent Garden. "Covent Garden is a very rarefied European style cuisine place, the owners all belong to this elite club of which I am not a member."

She has also called out the culture of bullying and sexual harassment in professional kitchens, and the absence of HR structures in most restaurants. Her response has been to build a mentoring program aimed at bringing women from minority backgrounds into leadership positions in hospitality.

Curry Houses, Immigration, and Respect

For Indian diaspora communities, Khan's argument strikes a familiar chord. The underpricing of Indian cuisine mirrors broader patterns in which South Asian contributions are consumed but not fully valued in Western societies. Khan has consistently linked food justice to immigration justice, arguing that diners cannot celebrate curry while remaining hostile to the communities that created it.

"I stand on the shoulders of the curry houses. Thank god for them that they did this in the 70s at a time when this country was so racist. But now the time has come that I expect us to be honoured."

— Asma Khan

"You cannot have my food and not have me," Khan told the Thomson Reuters Foundation. "My tasting menu is not just about food and my ego — it is about storytelling. I tell you a story about my people through the food so that when you get up from the table you may still not like someone who looks like me — I forgive you — but at least you'll understand where I come from."

What's Next

Darjeeling Express is preparing to move into a larger space on Rupert Street, a transition Khan sees as a chance to expand both the restaurant and its mission. The new location will house a deli serving Indian railway foods alongside the tasting menus, and a mentoring school for aspiring female restaurateurs from underrepresented backgrounds.

Khan is also set to deliver the SOAS Food Studies Centre Annual Distinguished Lecture, where she plans to address the "power politics of food" — from the exploitation of farmers growing jackfruit for Western vegan markets to the environmental cost of culinary trends like the global matcha craze.

Nearly a decade after opening her doors, Khan's core message remains the same: respect for the food requires respect for the people behind it.
nri_angle: Khan's fight against the undervaluation of Indian cuisine reflects a broader pattern diaspora communities recognize — South Asian cultural contributions consumed but not fully respected in Western societies.
